source.title: Research Report: Alternative sparsity methods for sparse autoencoders with OthelloGPT.

record.tranche_reason: The study applies sparse autoencoders to OthelloGPT and reports how many board-position classifiers their features recover, extending evidence about SAE feature recovery to this model and benchmark. It does not test the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports classifier counts for selected SAEs under different sparsity methods. Cited results from Robert's separate report are not included as rows. Gray datapoints not evaluated for good classifiers and unquantified statements about early variations are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs on OthelloGPT as a tool and compares its own sparsity methods (smoothed-L0, freshman's dream, without-top-k, leaky top-k, dimension reduction) against an L1 baseline. Its metric is the count of board-position classifiers with AUROC above 0.9. It asks which method finds more classifiers, not whether superposition exists, whether features spread across neurons, or whether SAE features are the model's units. The 180-pair denominator and the linear-probe comparison come from Robert_AIZI's cited report, not this study. So the rows are performance comparisons of the study's own methods, not tests of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Smoothed-L0, leaky top-k (45 best) and dimension reduction beat L1 (29); without-top-k was on par and freshman's dream was worse. The author treats these as exploratory leads, not strong evidence to replace L1.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains SAEs with alternative sparsity losses and activation functions on OthelloGPT residual-stream activations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported classifier count varies with sparsity method and its hyperparameters; the author also reports dead neurons for all tested leaky top-k SAEs with ϵ=0 and none for those with ϵ>0.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features on OthelloGPT layer-3 residuals give good board-position classifiers for only 21–45 pairs, depending on sparsity method. The author notes linear probes classify most of the 180 pairs, citing Robert's report.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How many linearly probe-able features an SAE recovers depends strongly on the sparsity mechanism, and recovery stays incomplete.

record.problems: The author describes the hyperparameter search as intuitive and limited rather than exhaustive, evaluates selected promising SAEs rather than every trained SAE, and uses an AUROC threshold of 0.9 and a specialized Othello board-classification benchmark. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported classifier counts.
record.rows_left_out: No classifier-count results were left out. Sparsity percentages, unexplained variance, and dead-neuron figures are mentioned in row notes where reported, but are not separate rows because they do not themselves measure SAE recovery of board-position classifiers.

untested.parts: Toy-model geometry and the sparsity-dependent transition are not studied.
The capacity account of polysemanticity is not studied.
Other causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
There is no test of features spreading across neurons or of sparse-feature recovery as evidence of superposition. SAE classifier counts are used only to rank sparsity methods.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not assessed. The incomplete recovery is not framed as bearing on this.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T3' with V4 labels is overturned. The study is an SAE-methods benchmark that relies on SAEs as a tool. The author also hypothesizes that OthelloGPT may not represent the board in fully factorized positions, but this is speculation, not a result.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test toy-model superposition, overlap geometry, or a sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from competition for representational capacity.
The study does not investigate causes of polysemantic neurons.
It tests SAE recovery of board-position classifiers in OthelloGPT, not whether features spread across neurons in general LLMs or whether SAEs recover other kinds of features across real LLMs.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions.
